name: Yanghua (拍洋画)
blurb: Flipping paper picture cards with a slap of air: win your friend's card if it turns over
title: What Is Pai Yanghua (拍洋画)? China's Picture Card Flipping Game
description: Pai yanghua (拍洋画) is a Chinese children's game: slap the ground beside a paper picture card so the gust flips it and you win it. Huge in the 1980s–90s.
answer: Pai yanghua (拍洋画, slapping foreign pictures) is a Chinese children's game played with small printed paper cards. One player lays a card on the ground; the other slaps the ground beside it, or throws down their own card, so the rush of air flips it over, and a flipped card is won. The cards showed heroes from Three Kingdoms, Journey to the West and other stories, or animals. It was everywhere in the 1980s and 1990s, faded with video games, and a near-identical game with cigarette-pack cards swept Chinese primary schools in 2024.

body: Yanghua were stiff paper cards about the size of a matchbox, colour-printed on the front. Popular sets showed famous generals and characters from classic novels, animal series, or numbers, Chinese chess pieces and playing-card suits that could be compared. Rare designs were worth more. In many places they came printed on a whole sheet that you cut apart yourself.

ol: One player puts one or more cards face up on flat ground
The other slaps the ground right beside a card with a cupped hand, or slams down their own card, so the air flips it
A flipped card goes to the slapper; if nothing turns over, it is the other player's turn

body: Local variations abound: flipping two at once, everyone putting in a few cards and taking turns, or only face-up to face-down counting. Similar games exist elsewhere: menko in Japan and ddakji in Korea.

No one knows exactly. The usual explanation is that when Western cigarettes came to China, some packs included small picture cards, called cigarette cards (香烟牌子) in Shanghai; imitations followed, printed with foreigners, ships and guns, so they became yanghua, foreign pictures. Names vary by region: yanghuar, yangpian or huapian in the north, 公仔纸 in Cantonese-speaking areas, and 尪仔标, often round, in Taiwan.

Video games and branded trading cards pushed it aside from the 2000s. In 2024, cards cut and folded from cigarette packets, called yanka, became a craze among primary school pupils in many parts of China, played exactly like yanghua. Because the cards come from cigarette packaging, China News Service and other media reported that education authorities in several places urged parents and schools to steer children away from the game.

faq.q: How is yanghua different from yanka?
faq.a: The game is the same. Yanghua were printed picture cards; yanka are cut from cigarette packs, which is why the 2024 craze worried parents and schools.
Yes. Menko is also played by flipping an opponent's card on the ground; ddakji in Korea is similar too.

faq.q: What is the trick to flipping a card?
faq.a: Players say to cup your hand and slap right at the card's edge so the air gets underneath; flat cards are harder to flip than bent ones.
